title: Quinoa vs. rice: protein, fiber, and carbs

seo.title: Quinoa vs. rice: protein, fiber, and carbs
seo.meta_description: Cooked quinoa provides more protein and fiber and fewer carbs than cooked white rice at similar calories. Compare per 100 g and per serving.
seo.search_intent: Compare quinoa and rice for protein, fiber, carbs, calories, amino acids, and micronutrients.

excerpt: Cooked quinoa provides more protein and fiber than white rice at similar calories: about 4.4 grams of protein and 2.8 grams of fiber per 100 grams versus roughly 2.7 grams and 0.4 gram. It also has fewer carbs, about 21 grams versus 28. The advantage is real, but a serving of quinoa still functions more like a grain base than a main protein source.
content_html:
Quinoa is often presented as a “much higher-protein” alternative to rice. It does contain more protein, but the size of the difference matters: roughly 1.5–2 extra grams per 100 grams cooked. That is useful, but it does not turn quinoa into a direct substitute for beans, tofu, eggs, fish or meat.

Its broader advantage over white rice is the combination of a little more protein, much more fiber and more minerals at fairly similar calories.

Start with the cooked comparison

Per 100 g cookedQuinoaWhite rice
Calories~120~130
Protein~4.4 g~2.7 g
Carbohydrate~21 g~28 g
Fiber~2.8 g~0.4 g
Fat~1.9 g~0.3 g

Quinoa provides about 10 fewer calories, 1.7 extra grams of protein and roughly 2.4 extra grams of fiber per 100 grams. Proportionally, fiber is the difference that really stands out.

A serving shows what those grams actually mean

One cooked cup of quinoa, about 185 grams, provides roughly 8 grams of protein and 5 grams of fiber. A similar volume of cooked white rice, around 180 grams, provides close to 5 grams of protein and less than 1 gram of fiber.

Adding 3 extra grams of protein and several grams of fiber is useful. But if the meal needs 25–30 grams of protein, neither base gets there on its own; a more concentrated protein source still has to do most of that work.

“Complete protein” describes quality, not quantity

Quinoa contains all nine essential amino acids in an especially balanced profile for a starch-rich plant food. That is a genuine nutritional strength.

But a protein can be complete and still be present in a modest amount. At about 4.4 grams per 100 grams cooked, quinoa behaves more like a pseudocereal on the plate than a main protein food.

Quinoa also has a mineral advantage

A cooked cup can provide around 100–120 mg of magnesium along with iron, phosphorus, manganese and folate. Refined white rice generally provides less of several of these nutrients, although enrichment can change iron and B-vitamin values in U.S. products.

The comparison changes with brown rice

Brown rice keeps the bran and germ, so it provides more fiber and magnesium than white rice. That narrows the gap with quinoa considerably.

Quinoa still usually has a modest edge in protein and fiber per 100 grams cooked, but the comparison is no longer nearly as one-sided. That is why specific numbers should say what kind of rice is being compared.

Both are naturally gluten-free

Neither quinoa nor rice naturally contains gluten. For people with celiac disease, the practical issue is cross-contact and choosing appropriately labeled products when needed.

Which should you choose?

If you want more fiber, a little more protein and greater mineral density, quinoa has an advantage over white rice. If you want a low-cost, neutral, easy-to-digest and highly versatile starch, rice remains a perfectly good staple.

Quinoa improves several nutrients, but it does not turn a starchy side dish into a high-protein meal by itself. The rest of the plate still decides that.

faq.question: Which has more protein, quinoa or rice?
faq.answer: Cooked quinoa provides about 4.4 g protein per 100 g versus roughly 2.7 g in cooked white rice.

faq.question: Which has more fiber?
faq.answer: Quinoa is around 2.8 g fiber per 100 g cooked versus roughly 0.4 g in white rice. Brown rice narrows part of that gap.

faq.question: Can quinoa replace meat as a protein source?
faq.answer: Not by quantity. Its protein is complete, but at about 4.4 g per 100 g cooked it is far less protein-dense than tofu, legumes, eggs, fish, or meat.
